title: US and Denmark Seal a Greenland Security Deal as UN Experts Cite War Crimes in America's Iran Strikes
subhead: Washington and Copenhagen resolve the year-long annexation standoff with a security pact granting the US permanent basing rights over the Arctic territory, while a UN fact-finding mission says it has reasonable grounds to believe US strikes on Iranian civilians were war crimes.

sections.heading: Greenland: Washington and Copenhagen Turn a Territorial Crisis Into a Security Pact
sections.body:
The United States and Denmark announced a deal on Greenland's security, defusing a diplomatic crisis that began when President Donald Trump threatened to take the mineral-rich Danish territory by force. Trump said in a social media post that the agreement gives the US 'permanent control over security, and all other needs' in Greenland at 'no cost to the United States'. Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the agreement 'strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area' while recognising Denmark's sovereignty and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination. The deal is to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week and will need legislative approval in Denmark and Greenland.

An unnamed US State Department official briefed that the pact grants Washington unilateral authority to build additional military structures without approval from Denmark or Greenland, with 'permanent access, basing and overflights rights'. It bans non-NATO countries from establishing bases in Greenland and bars adversaries from making investments there that could threaten the United States. Crucially, the official said the deal would not expire even if Greenland were to become independent. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it 'a historic deal' that 'permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns'. The agreement's full text has not been released, and Danish officials have not confirmed the specifics Trump outlined.
sections.whyItMatters: This converts a destabilising confrontation between two NATO allies into a legal framework that locks American military primacy over the Arctic's key landmass — and sets a precedent for how the US secures chokepoints and mineral resources in the far north against Russian and Chinese access.

sections.heading: Trump Signs Sweeping Russia Sanctions Backed by Rare Bipartisan Support
sections.body:
President Trump signed into law the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, the first major Ukraine-related bill to clear Congress in more than two years. Named for the late Republican senator who negotiated it before his death in July, and co-written with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, the law sanctions Vladimir Putin, senior officials, oligarchs, Russian banks, energy and defence sectors, and the shadow fleet of tankers used to move Russian oil. Al Jazeera reports its central provision empowers Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas — a measure expected to hit China and India hardest, the top two importers of Russian crude. The bill also extends sanctions on Iran's energy and weapons sectors.

The legislation passed the House on Wednesday with 58 Democrats crossing party lines. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who lobbied lawmakers directly, called it 'an extremely powerful tool'. House Speaker Mike Johnson said it placed 'maximum pressure' on the Russian war machine. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries opposed the bill, warning its tariff powers would raise costs for American families and calling its sanctions provisions full of 'loopholes'. The signing follows Russia and China vetoing a UN mandate to monitor Iran sanctions earlier in the week, per Al Jazeera.
sections.whyItMatters: The tariff mechanism aimed at Chinese and Indian purchases of Russian crude is the most consequential move yet in the effort to starve Moscow of war revenue — and it risks a direct commercial confrontation with the two largest buyers sustaining Russia's oil exports.

sections.heading: Macron Warns Russian Hybrid Attacks on Europe Are Intensifying
sections.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron said the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans has 'intensified' in recent weeks, telling journalists after meeting party leaders that 'the intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine'. The BBC reports Macron said he has tasked the government with protecting critical infrastructure and defence industry sites. He cited last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany, blamed on Russia, and warnings from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Tusk told Polish MPs that Russian plans included drone and missile strikes on countries supporting Ukraine, warning there was a 'real risk' of strikes on NATO territory that Moscow would then claim were 'accidental' in an attempt to split the alliance.

Macron framed the pressure as counterproductive: 'We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine.' The warnings follow a Russian drone strike on a passenger train near the Ukraine-Poland border last Sunday, shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed along the same line. Ukraine said all passengers were evacuated minutes before the strike.
sections.whyItMatters: Western leaders are publicly validating that Russia is moving beyond the battlefield into sabotage and infrastructure attacks on NATO territory — forcing European governments to shift resources toward homeland defence even as they sustain support for Ukraine.

sections.heading: UN Experts Say There Are Grounds to Believe US Committed War Crimes in Iran Strikes
sections.body:
A UN fact-finding mission on Iran told the Human Rights Council it has 'reasonable grounds to believe that the US committed the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack' in two of the deadliest civilian incidents of the conflict. The BBC reports the mission investigated strikes on 28 February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran. At Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the southern town of Minab, Tomahawk missiles killed at least 156 people, including 120 children, according to local authorities. The experts said the school was adjacent to an IRGC naval complex that was also attacked, but that the school was clearly identifiable and showed no sign of military use; media reports indicated a preliminary US military inquiry found US forces responsible.

The mission also concluded the school was 'the intended point of impact', citing survivors who said it was struck twice, rather than collateral damage from the attack on the base. At Lamerd, Precision Strike Missiles dispersed tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area, killing at least 21 civilians including seven children. The US military has not released its findings on the Minab strike; Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said the US would 'never target civilian targets', and the military disputes the weapon identification at Lamerd. The experts warned that civilians in Iran are 'caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel'.
sections.whyItMatters: A formal UN body now asserts credible evidence that the US struck what it regards as clearly identifiable civilian sites with mass casualties — placing legal and reputational pressure on Washington in the Iran war even as the conflict continues at scale.

sections.heading: Suicide Bombing Kills 21 at a Mosque in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
sections.body:
A car bomb detonated at a mosque inside a police compound in Kohat, in north-western Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, killing at least 21 people and injuring more than 100, officials told the BBC. Fifteen police officers and a four-year-old child were among those killed. A car loaded with explosives rammed the mosque's entrance at about 13:15 local time during Friday prayers, with gunmen firing on the police facility in a coordinated suicide attack. At least six attackers were killed in the blast and the ensuing gun battle, according to a provincial police spokesperson. Pakistan's APP news agency reported the attack; BBC Verify located video showing the site covered in rubble.

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Police suggested a faction of the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as the Pakistani Taliban, carried out the attack. The group, founded in 2007 and allied with al-Qaeda and the Afghan Taliban, is the designated target of Pakistan's ongoing counter-insurgency push. President Asif Ali Zardari offered condolences and called for the 'complete elimination' of foreign-backed terrorists. The attack follows this week's collision of Indian and Pakistani warships in the Arabian Sea, keeping South Asian security and the Kashmir-adjacent tribal belt in focus simultaneously.
sections.whyItMatters: The TTP's demonstrated ability to strike a fortified police compound during Friday prayers underscores the persistent insurgency threat along Pakistan's Afghan border — and complicates Islamabad's security posture as it manages simultaneous friction with both India and the Taliban-linked groups to its west.

bottomLine: The most significant development of the day is diplomatic, not military: Washington and Copenhagen converted months of annexation threats into a Greenland security pact that locks in permanent American basing and excludes both non-NATO bases and adversary investment over the Arctic's strategic landmass, to be signed at next week's UN General Assembly. Alongside that, Trump signed sweeping Russia sanctions that for the first time directly threaten China and India's purchases of Russian crude, European leaders publicly confirmed an intensifying Russian hybrid campaign against NATO infrastructure, and a UN body asserted credible grounds that the US committed war crimes in two strikes on Iranian civilians. The Pakistan mosque massacre was a reminder that the TTP insurgency remains a live threat on NATO's southern periphery. Together these developments point to a day defined less by battlefield movement than by legal and economic escalation across several fronts at once.
